lesson.title: SLIs SLOs error budgets and reliability targets
lesson.why: Reliability decisions need an explicit user-facing target. Otherwise teams argue over individual failures without knowing whether the service is meeting its promise.
lesson.what: Define eligible events, a good-event indicator, an objective window, and an error-budget response policy.

concepts.name: Indicator definition
concepts.body: An SLI measures service behavior such as successful requests or latency below a threshold. Define eligibility and measurement location carefully. Excluding failed requests from the denominator makes a success ratio look better precisely when users are suffering.

concepts.name: Objective window
concepts.body: An SLO sets a target over a stated window and population. Rolling windows and calendar windows behave differently around boundaries. Choose targets from user needs and dependency reality rather than copying a vendor availability percentage without checking what it measures.

concepts.name: Error budget
concepts.body: The budget is the allowed amount of bad behavior under the objective. It is not permission to ignore individual incidents or security failures. A policy connects consumption to release caution, investigation, and reliability investment while leaving room for useful product changes.

concepts.name: Burn rate
concepts.body: Burn rate compares observed bad-event fraction with the allowed fraction. Sustained rapid burn threatens the window's budget before a long-window average looks alarming. Multiple windows help distinguish urgent sustained impact from short noisy spikes and slow persistent degradation.

e2e: Define eligible user events and the exact good-event condition.
Measure the indicator over the objective's agreed population and window.
Compare bad events with the allowed budget and calculate burn.
Apply a documented response policy and revisit measurement gaps after incidents.

tasks.name: Calculate a request budget
steps: For one million eligible requests and a 99.9 percent success SLO, allowed failures are 1000000*0.001=1000. If 600 failures occurred, 400 remain. This is request-based accounting, not a claim that a fixed number of downtime minutes was consumed.

tasks.name: Compute burn rate
steps: Allowed bad fraction is 0.1 percent; observed bad fraction over a short window is 1 percent. Burn rate is 1/0.1=10 times. Explain why the short-window rate does not alone reveal the total remaining monthly budget without request volume and previous consumption.

tasks.name: Review eligibility
steps: A checkout SLI counts only responses that returned before a timeout. Add timed-out eligible requests to the denominator and bad-event numerator. Decide how client cancellations and invalid input are classified before implementation, then document the user impact represented by those choices.

tasks.name: Design a budget policy
steps: For a fictional team, define actions for rapid burn and near-exhaustion: investigate, pause risky releases, and prioritize a demonstrated reliability fix. Preserve emergency repair paths. Explain why a blanket permanent feature freeze is not a useful substitute for a measured policy.

key_terms: SLI: measured service behavior.
SLO: target for a defined indicator.
Error budget: allowed bad-event quantity.
Burn rate: observed failure fraction divided by allowed fraction.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic counts; do not change live reliability targets or paging policies.
cleanup: Discard the budget worksheet; no monitoring rules changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a service meets its monthly average while users suffer a sharp outage. How would budget burn improve detection?
interview_points: Define eligible user failures consistently.
Compare short and long windows against allowed failure fraction.
Route sustained rapid burn to a concrete response policy.

storyboard.title: Rapid burn can hide inside a healthy monthly average
storyboard.objective: Connect short-window impact with budget risk.

scenes.title: Measure the objective
scenes.caption: The denominator includes eligible failures.
scenes.narration: Request outcomes determine how much of the agreed error budget is consumed.

scenes.title: Burn accelerates
scenes.caption: A short outage spends budget quickly.
scenes.narration: The current failure fraction exceeds the allowed fraction despite a healthy long-window average.

scenes.title: Act on the policy
scenes.caption: Urgency follows measured impact.
scenes.narration: Sustained rapid burn triggers investigation and controlled release decisions.

sre/slis-slos-error-budgets-and-reliabil.core: Define SLI eligibility, SLO target and window, then calculate budget and burn. Use multi-window evidence and an explicit policy rather than treating reliability percentages as slogans.

lesson.title: Incident command triage communication and escalation
lesson.why: During an outage, uncoordinated experts can make conflicting changes. Clear roles and evidence-based communication reduce confusion while mitigation proceeds.
lesson.what: Organize incident command, technical triage, stakeholder updates, and escalation around a hypothetical service failure.

concepts.name: Incident command
concepts.body: The incident commander coordinates priorities, ownership, and decisions rather than personally performing every repair. Separate operations, communications, and recording when staffing permits. Explicit handoffs prevent duplicate work and keep a long-running incident from depending on one exhausted responder.

concepts.name: Triage and mitigation
concepts.body: First determine user impact, scope, timing, and recent changes. Prefer reversible mitigations supported by evidence while preserving diagnostic data. The immediate goal is service recovery, not a complete root-cause theory; record uncertainty instead of delaying action until every detail is known.

concepts.name: Communication cadence
concepts.body: Updates should state confirmed impact, current actions, known uncertainty, and the next update time. Avoid invented recovery estimates or unsupported causal claims. Internal technical detail and external customer communication have different audiences and privacy requirements.

concepts.name: Escalation criteria
concepts.body: Escalate when impact, expertise gaps, time, or authority requirements exceed the current team's ability. Predefined contacts and severity criteria shorten delay. Escalation is a coordination tool, not a personal failure, and responders need permission to stop unsafe changes.

e2e: A responder confirms impact and opens an incident with a clear owner.
Command assigns technical, communication, and timeline responsibilities.
Operators test bounded hypotheses and apply reversible mitigation.
Health evidence confirms recovery, stakeholders are updated, and follow-up ownership is recorded.

tasks.name: Build a factual timeline
steps: Record alert at 14:02, confirmed checkout failures at 14:04, mitigation at 14:11, and verified recovery at 14:16. Detection-to-verification is fourteen minutes. Mark a 13:58 deployment as a candidate correlation, not established cause, until evidence supports that conclusion.

tasks.name: Assign incident roles
steps: With four fictional responders, assign commander, operations lead, communications lead, and recorder. Have the operator announce a proposed rollback and its stop condition before execution. Explain how command prevents another responder from simultaneously changing database capacity without coordination.

tasks.name: Write an honest update
steps: Draft a message stating affected checkout requests, investigation of a recent change, mitigation underway, and a next update in ten minutes. Do not claim customer data loss or a precise recovery time without evidence. Identify what additional fact would change the severity assessment.

tasks.name: Choose escalation triggers
steps: The team cannot verify whether database promotion is safe. Escalate to the data owner before promotion, preserve the current writer state, and document the required decision. Contrast this with paging every specialist immediately, which may increase coordination load without improving the specific missing expertise.

key_terms: Incident commander: coordination owner.
Triage: initial impact and scope assessment.
Mitigation: action reducing current harm.
Escalation: obtaining needed expertise or authority.
lesson.safety: Use a tabletop incident only; do not page people, alter production, or publish fictional status updates.
cleanup: Discard the synthetic timeline and messages; no real incident records changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, three responders are making different changes during an outage. How would you restore coordination without stopping useful work?
interview_points: Establish command and explicit operation ownership.
Record hypotheses, changes, and stop conditions.
Maintain factual updates and targeted escalation.

scenes.title: Assign responsibilities
scenes.caption: One operation owner coordinates changes.
scenes.narration: Command establishes who will mitigate and who will communicate confirmed facts.

scenes.title: Conflicting proposals appear
scenes.caption: Uncoordinated actions increase uncertainty.
scenes.narration: Simultaneous rollback and database changes require an explicit sequencing decision.

scenes.title: Execute a bounded plan
scenes.caption: Record evidence and next update time.
scenes.narration: The agreed mitigation proceeds while communications report impact and uncertainty accurately.

sre/incident-command-triage-communicatio.core: Establish command, operations, communication, and a timeline. Prioritize reversible mitigation, preserve evidence, state uncertainty honestly, and escalate specific expertise or authority gaps.

lesson.title: Blameless postmortems and corrective actions
lesson.why: A postmortem should improve the system that shaped decisions, not merely identify the last person who touched it. Learning requires accurate evidence and owned follow-through.
lesson.what: Build a causal account, identify contributing conditions, and choose verifiable corrective actions from a fictional outage.

concepts.name: Blameless inquiry
concepts.body: Blamelessness means examining why actions made sense with the information and constraints available. It does not remove responsibility for repairs or honest reporting. Avoid hindsight assumptions that responders knew facts discovered only after the incident.

concepts.name: Causal structure
concepts.body: Separate trigger, contributing conditions, detection gaps, and recovery obstacles. Complex incidents rarely have one sufficient cause. A deployment may trigger failure while missing validation, weak isolation, and poor rollback capability determine the size and duration of impact.

concepts.name: Action quality
concepts.body: Strong actions change a system or process and have an owner, deadline, priority, and acceptance test. Be more careful is not measurable. Prefer eliminating a risky path or automating a check over adding another reminder that depends on perfect human attention.

concepts.name: Learning verification
concepts.body: Review action completion and test whether the intended risk is actually reduced. Counting closed tickets is weaker than reproducing the failure mode safely and observing containment. Share relevant lessons across teams without exposing personal data or turning the narrative into performance blame.

e2e: Collect a factual incident timeline and quantify user impact.
Reconstruct decisions using the information available at each point.
Map triggers and contributing system conditions without personal blame.
Assign and verify corrective actions, then track whether the failure mode is better controlled.

tasks.name: Calculate impact honestly
tasks.goal: Separate outage duration from failed requests.
steps: A twenty-minute incident handled 40000 requests, of which 6000 failed. Failure fraction is 15 percent. Report both twenty-minute incident duration and 6000 failed requests rather than claiming all users were unavailable for twenty minutes or averaging away the impact.

tasks.name: Build a causal chain
steps: A configuration typo reached production, rollback lacked a retained artifact, and detection took ten minutes. Identify trigger, prevention gap, recovery gap, and detection gap separately. Explain why naming only the person who approved the typo would leave most of the mechanism unchanged.

tasks.name: Rewrite a weak action
steps: Replace remind engineers to check ports with add a rendered Service-to-container port contract test owned by the platform team. Define acceptance as a deliberate mismatched-port fixture failing CI. Include a deadline and explain which failure this test cannot catch, such as runtime network policy denial.

tasks.name: Validate learning completion
tasks.goal: Measure reduced risk rather than ticket closure.
steps: A rollback-artifact retention action is marked done. Require a disposable drill that retrieves the previous digest and restores compatible behavior within the target time. Record any data compatibility limitation and keep the action open if the artifact exists but cannot actually be deployed.

key_terms: Trigger: event initiating the incident sequence.
Contributing condition: factor increasing likelihood or impact.
Corrective action: owned measurable risk reduction.
Acceptance test: evidence that an action works.
lesson.safety: Use invented incidents and roles; do not publish real personnel details or confidential incident records.
cleanup: Discard the synthetic causal map; no real action tracker was modified.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a postmortem concludes that an engineer should have been more careful. How would you turn it into useful system improvements?
interview_points: Reconstruct information and constraints without hindsight blame.
Identify prevention, detection, and recovery contributors.
Assign measurable actions and verify reduced failure impact.

storyboard.title: Learning extends beyond the triggering mistake
storyboard.objective: Translate causal evidence into verifiable actions.

scenes.title: Reconstruct events
scenes.caption: Use what responders knew then.
scenes.narration: The timeline separates observed facts from conclusions discovered later.

scenes.title: Find multiple contributors
scenes.caption: The typo was not the whole system.
scenes.narration: Missing validation and unavailable rollback artifacts amplified the triggering change.

scenes.title: Verify improvement
scenes.caption: A closed ticket is not enough.
scenes.narration: A failing contract fixture and successful recovery drill prove specific corrective actions work.

sre/blameless-postmortems-and-corrective.core: Blameless analysis reconstructs decisions and system conditions. Separate triggers from amplifiers, assign owned measurable actions, and verify risk reduction through tests or drills.

lesson.title: Reliability patterns timeouts retries jitter and circuit breakers
lesson.why: Retries can amplify an outage instead of recovering from it. Reliable clients must bound total work and distinguish transient failure from unsafe repetition.
lesson.what: Design deadlines, retry budgets, backoff, jitter, and circuit-breaker behavior using an offline request timeline.

concepts.name: Deadline allocation
concepts.body: A timeout bounds one wait; an end-to-end deadline bounds the whole operation. Allocate connection, execution, and retry time within the caller's remaining budget. Continuing expensive work after the caller has abandoned the request wastes capacity and can cause surprising side effects.

concepts.name: Retry safety
concepts.body: Retry transient failures only when the operation is safe to repeat or protected by an idempotency contract. A timeout does not prove the server did nothing. Retrying an already committed payment without deduplication can create duplicate effects despite a well-behaved client library.

concepts.name: Backoff and jitter
concepts.body: Exponential backoff spaces repeated attempts while a maximum delay and attempt count bound cost. Jitter randomizes timing so many clients do not retry together. Retrying at every layer multiplies attempts; choose a responsible layer and propagate remaining deadlines.

concepts.name: Circuit breakers
concepts.body: A breaker temporarily rejects calls after observed failure thresholds, then allows limited probes during recovery. It prevents repeated pressure on a failing dependency but introduces state and tuning complexity. Distinguish breaker rejection from the original dependency error in telemetry.

e2e: The caller assigns a total deadline and safe retry policy.
A transient failure consumes part of that budget.
Bounded backoff with jitter schedules another safe attempt only if time remains.
Repeated failures open the breaker; limited recovery probes later restore calls.

tasks.name: Calculate retry amplification
steps: Three layers each allow three total attempts. One user operation can cause 3*3*3=27 lowest-level attempts in the worst case. If only the outer layer retries three times and inner layers attempt once, the bound becomes three. Specify total attempts, not ambiguous retry counts.

tasks.name: Allocate a deadline
steps: A request has a two-second total deadline. Two attempts of 700ms plus one 200ms backoff consume 1600ms before overhead. A third 700ms attempt cannot fit. Explain why giving each dependency its own fresh two-second timeout violates the caller's total budget.

tasks.name: Protect a write retry
steps: A server commits an order but the response is lost. Reuse the same synthetic idempotency key on retry and return the stored result. Define the key's scope and atomic recording requirement rather than generating a new key for every network attempt.

tasks.name: Plan breaker recovery
steps: Model closed, open, and half-open states for a dependency. Permit a small bounded number of probes after the open interval and return to open if they fail. Explain why allowing all queued callers immediately can overwhelm a dependency that has only partially recovered.

key_terms: Deadline: total operation time bound.
Backoff: increasing delay between attempts.
Jitter: randomized retry timing.
Circuit breaker: stateful temporary call rejection.
lesson.safety: Use paper timing and synthetic keys; do not induce real dependency failures or retry external writes.
cleanup: Discard the attempt tree; no service settings changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, retries increase sharply while a dependency recovers slowly. How would you reduce amplification without losing necessary operations?
interview_points: Bound total attempts at one responsible layer.
Respect end-to-end deadlines and idempotency.
Use jitter and limited recovery probes with distinct telemetry.

storyboard.title: Retries consume capacity and time budgets
storyboard.objective: Prevent recovery traffic from amplifying failure.

scenes.title: Attempt within budget
scenes.caption: Every attempt consumes remaining time.
scenes.narration: The client sends a safe request with a bounded deadline.

scenes.title: Stop repeated pressure
scenes.caption: The breaker rejects excess attempts.
scenes.narration: Repeated failures open the breaker instead of flooding the dependency.

scenes.title: Probe recovery gradually
scenes.caption: Do not release every caller at once.
scenes.narration: Limited successful probes restore calls without a synchronized retry surge.

sre/reliability-patterns-timeouts-retrie.core: Bound total deadlines and attempts, retry only safe operations, avoid layered amplification, add jitter, and use limited breaker probes. A timeout does not prove an operation was uncommitted.

lesson.title: Load shedding backpressure bulkheads and graceful degradation
lesson.why: Accepting more work than a system can finish turns overload into long queues and widespread failure. Controlled refusal can preserve useful service.
lesson.what: Compare admission limits, producer feedback, isolated resource pools, and optional-feature degradation using a capacity model.

concepts.name: Admission and shedding
concepts.body: Load shedding rejects or drops work before scarce resources are exhausted. Prioritize based on explicit product rules and provide appropriate retry guidance. Rejecting early is often better than accepting a request that will time out after consuming expensive downstream capacity.

concepts.name: Backpressure
concepts.body: Backpressure slows producers when consumers cannot keep up. It can propagate through bounded queues or flow-control protocols. A queue without a capacity limit is delayed failure rather than protection, and clients must actually respect feedback for the mechanism to work.

concepts.name: Bulkhead isolation
concepts.body: Separate pools or concurrency limits prevent one workload from consuming every worker, connection, or thread. Isolation reduces shared efficiency and requires sizing. A dedicated pool that is too small can reject healthy traffic while another pool has idle capacity.

concepts.name: Graceful degradation
concepts.body: Disable optional work while preserving core outcomes, such as omitting recommendations during checkout. Define truthful fallback behavior and consistency limits. Security checks, payment correctness, and access control are not optional features to skip when the system is busy.

e2e: Admission estimates available capacity before accepting additional work.
Bounded queues and feedback slow or reject excess demand.
Bulkheads contain saturation within the affected workload class.
Optional work degrades while core service remains measured and recovery is gradual.

tasks.name: Calculate queue growth
steps: Arrival rate is 120 requests per second and completion capacity is 100. Backlog grows by twenty per second. A 400-request empty queue fills in twenty seconds if rates stay constant. At full capacity, extra queue space only postpones overload and increases waiting time.

tasks.name: Design a core fallback
steps: A checkout request calls payment and recommendations. Keep payment authorization mandatory while allowing recommendations to return an explicit unavailable state. Explain why returning a fabricated payment success would violate correctness rather than constitute graceful degradation.

tasks.name: Allocate bulkheads
steps: A worker pool has twenty slots. Reserve twelve for interactive requests and eight for batch work in a simplified fixed partition. A batch surge cannot consume the twelve interactive slots, but unused batch slots cannot automatically help interactive work unless borrowing rules are deliberately implemented.

tasks.name: Review client feedback
steps: An overloaded endpoint returns a retryable response with bounded retry guidance. Require clients to respect deadlines, jitter, and attempt budgets. Explain why immediate infinite retries turn a protective shed decision into more arrival pressure and why some low-priority requests should not be retried at all.

key_terms: Load shedding: rejecting excess work early.
Backpressure: feedback slowing producers.
Bulkhead: isolated resource capacity.
Degradation: reduced optional functionality preserving core correctness.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic rates; do not saturate hosts, databases, or public endpoints.
cleanup: Discard the queue and pool worksheet; no limits were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, batch traffic exhausts connections and breaks checkout. Which overload controls would you add and what trade-offs follow?
interview_points: Bound queues and reject excess work early.
Isolate interactive and batch resources with measured capacity.
Preserve core correctness and constrain client retries.

storyboard.title: Isolate core requests from an overloaded batch pool

scenes.title: Route by workload class
scenes.caption: Pools have explicit capacity.
scenes.narration: Admission sends interactive and batch work to isolated resource pools.

scenes.title: Batch saturates
scenes.caption: Excess work is bounded or refused.
scenes.narration: The batch pool fills without consuming the interactive reservation.

scenes.title: Preserve core outcomes
scenes.caption: Shed optional demand and recover gradually.
scenes.narration: Interactive requests continue while batch producers slow down under bounded feedback.

sre/load-shedding-backpressure-bulkheads.core: Bound work before saturation. Shedding rejects, backpressure slows, bulkheads isolate, and degradation removes optional work. None should bypass core correctness or authorization.

lesson.title: Capacity planning load tests and bottleneck analysis
lesson.why: Capacity estimates based on average CPU can miss queueing, connection limits, and tail latency. Useful load tests reveal the first limiting resource under a representative workload.
lesson.what: Build an offline demand model and a bounded test plan with explicit success, stop, and interpretation criteria.

concepts.name: Demand model
concepts.body: Describe request mix, arrival rate, payload size, concurrency, and growth assumptions. Peak and burst demand differ from averages. A capacity forecast should include uncertainty and failure headroom rather than treating one benchmark number as a universal production limit.

concepts.name: Queueing behavior
concepts.body: As utilization approaches a constrained resource's capacity, waiting and tail latency often rise sharply. Little's Law relates average in-system work to throughput and average time under stable conditions. It is not a guarantee for rapidly changing or unstable queues.

concepts.name: Representative tests
concepts.body: Load tests need realistic operations and data distributions, not just a cheap health endpoint. Distinguish open arrival-rate models from closed concurrency models, which can reduce offered load when responses slow and therefore hide overload through coordinated omission.

concepts.name: Bottleneck evidence
concepts.body: Measure latency distributions, errors, throughput, queues, and resource saturation together. CPU, database locks, connection pools, and storage can each limit progress. Change one demonstrated constraint at a time and rerun the same workload before attributing improvement to a capacity increase.

e2e: Estimate demand and define service-level acceptance criteria.
Choose a representative bounded workload and isolated test environment.
Increase load in controlled steps while observing saturation and tail latency.
Identify the first limiting resource, change it deliberately, and validate the revised capacity.

tasks.name: Apply Little's Law
steps: At stable throughput of 200 requests per second and mean time in system of 0.25 seconds, average in-system requests are 200*0.25=50. If mean time rises to one second at the same throughput, the average becomes 200. This includes waiting, not just active CPU execution.

tasks.name: Calculate failure headroom
steps: Four replicas each safely handle fifty requests per second at the target latency. Total capacity is 200, but surviving one replica loss leaves 150. Plan a normal peak no higher than the demonstrated failure-safe capacity unless another mitigation or spare pool is available.

tasks.name: Diagnose a false CPU conclusion
steps: Throughput plateaus while CPU remains 30 percent, database connections are fully occupied, and queue wait rises. Investigate connection holding time and database latency before adding application CPU. Explain how extra replicas could worsen the shared database bottleneck.

tasks.name: Write safe test gates
steps: Define synthetic data, a maximum arrival rate, a ten-minute duration, an error threshold, and an immediate stop owner for a disposable environment. Include background dependencies in the scope. Do not run the test; explain why staging results still need production workload and topology caveats.

key_terms: Throughput: completed work per unit time.
Concurrency: work simultaneously in the system.
Saturation: resource demand reaching a limiting capacity.
Headroom: spare capacity for variation or failures.
lesson.safety: Perform calculations only; do not launch load generators or benchmark shared infrastructure.
cleanup: Discard the demand model; no test traffic or processes were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, adding application replicas raises database latency without increasing throughput. What would you measure and change next?
interview_points: Identify the shared bottleneck using queues and saturation.
Inspect connection usage and operation mix.
Retest one targeted change with failure headroom and tail-latency gates.

storyboard.title: More application capacity can worsen a shared bottleneck

scenes.title: Increase demand carefully
scenes.caption: Measure the whole request path.
scenes.narration: The workload increases while latency, errors, and dependency queues are observed.

scenes.title: Database saturates
scenes.caption: Application CPU can remain low.
scenes.narration: Requests wait for database capacity even though application replicas have spare CPU.

scenes.title: Fix the limiting resource
scenes.caption: Retest the same workload.
scenes.narration: A targeted connection or query improvement is validated before claiming more safe capacity.

sre/capacity-planning-load-tests-and-bot.core: Model demand, latency, and failure headroom together. Use representative bounded tests, distinguish arrival models, and fix demonstrated bottlenecks rather than scaling the easiest resource.

lesson.title: Disaster recovery RPO RTO backups and restore drills
lesson.why: A successful backup job does not prove recoverability. Recovery requires usable data, keys, dependencies, people, and an executable sequence under realistic constraints.
lesson.what: Translate business loss tolerances into backup and restore evidence using an offline disaster timeline.

concepts.name: Recovery point
concepts.body: RPO expresses acceptable data loss measured back from an incident to the recoverable point. Backup frequency is only one input: completion lag, replication delay, log availability, and application consistency affect the actual point that can be restored safely.

concepts.name: Recovery time
concepts.body: RTO measures acceptable restoration duration for the defined service outcome. Include detection, decision, provisioning, data restore, validation, and traffic cutover as applicable. Starting the clock only after the operator begins a restore hides real user impact.

concepts.name: Backup protection
concepts.body: Protect backups from the same failure or compromise that affects the source. Access separation, immutable retention where appropriate, key recovery, and independent locations reduce correlated loss. Replication alone can copy accidental deletion or corruption quickly and is not a complete backup strategy.

concepts.name: Restore verification
concepts.body: A drill should prove data integrity, application compatibility, and the ability to serve the required transaction. Restore into an isolated target, not over the only source copy. Measure achieved objectives and record dependency failures rather than declaring success when files merely download.

e2e: Define the business recovery outcome and acceptable data-loss window.
Capture protected consistent backups and retain required recovery dependencies.
Restore into an isolated environment and validate data plus application behavior.
Measure achieved RPO and RTO, then repair gaps before the next drill.

tasks.name: Compute achieved objectives
steps: An incident occurs at 09:00; the latest usable point is 08:52, giving eight minutes potential loss. Detection takes four minutes, approval six, restore twenty, validation eight, and cutover two. Sequential recovery is forty minutes. Compare with a five-minute RPO and thirty-minute RTO: both are missed.

tasks.name: Inventory hidden dependencies
steps: List encryption keys, restore credentials, database engine version, DNS authority, application image, and runbook access for a fictional service. Identify which reside in the same failed account as production and design an authorized independent recovery path for those dependencies.

tasks.name: Design an integrity check
tasks.goal: Validate meaning, not just file presence.
steps: Use a synthetic ledger with record IDs one through one hundred and a known total of 5050. A restored copy should match count, unique IDs, and sum, then pass an application read transaction. Explain why matching only the row count could miss altered amounts.

tasks.name: Plan a safe drill
steps: Restore a selected backup into an isolated target with outbound notifications disabled. Define success checks, abort criteria, cleanup ownership, and measured timestamps. Document any manual undocumented step as a reliability gap rather than allowing the expert operator's memory to become the recovery plan.

key_terms: RPO: acceptable recoverable data-loss interval.
RTO: acceptable service recovery duration.
Consistency: recoverable application-valid data state.
Restore drill: controlled proof of recovery capability.
lesson.safety: Use fictional backups; do not restore over existing data or activate customer-facing integrations.
cleanup: Discard the recovery worksheet; no backup copies or environments were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, backups are green but a restore misses the recovery target. What evidence would you collect and improve?
interview_points: Measure the full detection-to-service timeline.
Verify recoverable point, keys, versions, and dependencies.
Test application integrity and remove undocumented manual steps.

storyboard.title: Backup success is only the beginning of recovery

scenes.title: Select a usable point
scenes.caption: Account for completion and consistency.
scenes.narration: The recovery starts from the latest backup that can actually be restored.

scenes.title: Missing key blocks restore
scenes.caption: Stored bytes alone are insufficient.
scenes.narration: Unavailable decryption authority prevents progress despite a successful backup job.

scenes.title: Verify useful service
scenes.caption: Stop the clock after required checks.
scenes.narration: Recovered keys and validated data permit the application transaction that defines recovery.

sre/disaster-recovery-rpo-rto-backups-an.core: Measure actual recoverable points and end-to-end service restoration. Protect backups independently, preserve keys and artifacts, and prove data integrity through isolated restore drills.

lesson.title: Chaos engineering hypothesis and blast-radius control
lesson.why: Controlled failure experiments can expose weak assumptions, but uncontrolled disruption only creates incidents. Safety limits and falsifiable hypotheses come before fault injection.
lesson.what: Design a tabletop resilience experiment with measurable steady state, narrow scope, stop conditions, and recovery verification.

concepts.name: Hypothesis
concepts.body: State a specific expected behavior under a specific failure, such as maintaining checkout success when one stateless replica disappears. Define the measured population and tolerance. We expect resilience is too vague to be disproved or to guide an operational decision.

concepts.name: Blast radius
concepts.body: Limit affected users, resources, duration, and dependencies. Start in isolated environments and expand only with explicit authorization and evidence. A staging label alone does not prove isolation if the workload still calls production identity, messaging, or payment services.

concepts.name: Abort and recovery
concepts.body: An experiment needs independent monitoring, an immediate stop mechanism, and a tested restoration path. If the failure removes the same control channel needed to stop it, the abort design is weak. Assign one owner with authority to terminate the exercise.

concepts.name: Learning loop
concepts.body: Record observed behavior, deviations, and contributing conditions. A passed experiment validates only its tested scope and assumptions, not universal reliability. Convert failures into owned fixes and repeat the same bounded experiment to verify improvement before increasing scope.

e2e: Define a falsifiable resilience hypothesis and measurable steady state.
Verify isolation, authorization, blast radius, and independent abort controls.
Model or inject only the approved fault while observing user outcomes.
Restore normal conditions, verify recovery, and document bounded conclusions.

tasks.name: Calculate scope
steps: A fictional service has twenty replicas and the experiment affects one. Instance exposure is 1/20=5 percent, but user exposure need not be 5 percent because traffic and sessions may be uneven. Record both the resource bound and the user-impact measurement needed to validate the hypothesis.

tasks.name: Write a falsifiable hypothesis
steps: Propose that losing one stateless replica for two minutes keeps synthetic checkout success above 99 percent with remaining capacity. Specify request volume and latency bounds. Explain why no observed failures in only two requests would be weak supporting evidence.

tasks.name: Find hidden production paths
steps: A disposable environment uses production email and payment endpoints. Mark those dependencies outside the allowed experiment boundary and substitute synthetic sinks before any future test. Explain why only restricting the application namespace does not prevent external side effects.

tasks.name: Design an independent abort
steps: A planned network fault could disconnect the controller issuing recovery commands. Choose an out-of-band stop path and bounded automatic expiry, then define restoration verification. Do not run the fault; explain what evidence would be required before trusting the abort procedure.

key_terms: Steady state: measured normal service behavior.
Hypothesis: falsifiable expected failure response.
Blast radius: bounded affected scope.
Abort: immediate controlled experiment termination.
lesson.safety: This is a tabletop exercise only; do not kill processes, block networks, or inject real failures.
cleanup: Discard the experiment design; no fault injection or infrastructure change occurred.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a team wants to test resilience by shutting down random production nodes. What must change before the experiment is safe?
interview_points: Replace randomness with a bounded explicit hypothesis and scope.
Verify independent stop controls and external dependency isolation.
Start with low-risk evidence and document limited conclusions.

storyboard.title: The stop path must survive the injected fault
storyboard.objective: Make experiment safety independent of the tested component.

scenes.caption: A hypothesis names the affected target.
scenes.narration: The experiment specifies a disposable target, duration, and measurable outcome.

scenes.caption: The fault must not disable its own stop path.

sre/chaos-engineering-hypothesis-and-bla.core: Chaos experiments need falsifiable hypotheses, verified isolation, bounded exposure, independent abort controls, and recovery evidence. A pass supports only the tested scope.

lesson.title: Toil reduction runbooks and production readiness
lesson.why: Repeated manual work consumes engineering capacity and introduces inconsistent decisions. Automation helps only when the underlying procedure and failure handling are understood.
lesson.what: Identify toil, improve a runbook, and design a production-readiness review with measurable operational outcomes.

concepts.name: Toil characteristics
concepts.body: Toil is repetitive operational work that scales with service demand and produces little lasting improvement. Not every manual task is toil: investigation and design can create durable knowledge. Measure frequency, effort, and error risk before deciding which work deserves automation.

concepts.name: Runbook contracts
concepts.body: A useful runbook states symptoms, scope, prerequisites, safe diagnostic steps, decision points, stop conditions, and escalation. Commands need context and expected output. Blind command lists are risky when the same symptom has several causes or when the target environment is ambiguous.

concepts.name: Safe automation
concepts.body: Automate a well-understood bounded workflow with idempotency, dry-run support where meaningful, audit output, and failure recovery. Preserve human approval for high-impact ambiguous decisions. A script that performs mistakes faster is not a reliability improvement.

concepts.name: Readiness evidence
concepts.body: Production readiness covers ownership, service indicators, capacity, dependencies, security boundaries, deployment recovery, and tested operational procedures. It is not a one-time checklist certificate. Revisit evidence when architecture, traffic, or team ownership changes materially.

e2e: Measure repeated operational work and identify a high-value bounded candidate.
Document its decision logic and expected outcomes in a runbook.
Automate safe repeated steps while retaining explicit uncertainty and approval boundaries.
Verify reduced effort and errors, then maintain readiness evidence as the service evolves.

tasks.name: Calculate toil cost
steps: A task takes twelve minutes and occurs fifteen times per week: 180 minutes or three hours weekly. An automation taking eight hours to build with ten minutes weekly maintenance saves 170 minutes weekly. Simple payback is 480/170, about 2.82 weeks, excluding review and risk costs.

tasks.name: Repair a vague runbook
steps: Replace restart the service when slow with checks for error rate, queue depth, dependency latency, and recent changes. Include the expected healthy pattern and a stop condition before restart. Explain why a restart may erase evidence or increase pressure when the true cause is downstream saturation.

tasks.name: Define automation boundaries
steps: Automate gathering synthetic status and proposing a bounded restart plan, but require approval when data loss or writer failover is possible. Include a stable operation identifier and structured result. Explain how retries detect prior completion instead of duplicating an external action.

tasks.name: Review production readiness
steps: For a fictional API, request an owner, SLO, load-test result, dependency inventory, rollback artifact, and restore drill. Mark missing evidence with a risk owner and deadline. Explain why a signed checklist cannot compensate for an untested database recovery path.

key_terms: Toil: repetitive low-durability operational work.
Runbook: actionable bounded operational procedure.
Readiness review: evidence-based operational assessment.
Payback: time for savings to offset investment.
lesson.safety: Use hypothetical workflows; do not restart services, automate real changes, or access production credentials.
cleanup: Discard the toil worksheet and sample runbook outline.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a team wants to automate a frequently used restart command. What would you establish before building the script?
interview_points: Measure frequency, effort, and demonstrated causes.
Document safe target selection, decisions, and stop conditions.
Automate only understood actions with idempotency and verification.

storyboard.title: Automate a proven procedure, not an unexplained habit
storyboard.objective: Connect toil measurement with safe operational logic.

scenes.title: Measure repeated effort
scenes.caption: Frequency reveals an improvement candidate.
scenes.narration: The team measures recurring restart work and its operational risks.

scenes.title: Find an ambiguous cause
scenes.caption: Restart is not always the right response.
scenes.narration: Dependency saturation requires a different action, so the procedure needs decision points.

scenes.title: Encode validated steps
scenes.caption: Verification remains part of automation.
scenes.narration: Only understood bounded steps are automated with explicit stop and recovery behavior.

sre/toil-reduction-runbooks-and-producti.core: Measure toil, document decision logic, and automate bounded repeatable actions with verification. Production readiness requires current evidence of ownership, observability, capacity, and recovery.

lesson.title: Availability design and dependency failure
lesson.why: Adding replicas does not remove a shared dependency or correlated failure. Availability design starts with the complete request path and required outcomes.
lesson.what: Analyze serial dependencies, redundancy, common causes, and degraded modes with explicit assumptions rather than optimistic percentage multiplication.

concepts.name: Series dependencies
concepts.body: If a request requires every dependency, any required component can fail the operation. Multiplying availability estimates is valid only under specified independence and measurement assumptions. Shared region, identity, or deployment systems often violate independence and make simple estimates optimistic.

concepts.name: Redundant paths
concepts.body: Parallel replicas can tolerate individual failures when routing detects faults and surviving capacity is sufficient. Redundancy is ineffective if all replicas share the same unavailable database, configuration defect, or exhausted quota. Count failure domains, not just process instances.

concepts.name: Timeout and fallback
concepts.body: Optional dependencies can be removed from the critical path through bounded timeouts and truthful fallback. Cached data needs freshness and correctness limits. An authentication or payment dependency cannot be bypassed merely to improve an availability dashboard.

concepts.name: Recovery design
concepts.body: Detection, failover, warmup, and data consistency determine actual recovery behavior. Automatic failover may trade downtime for split-brain risk unless writer ownership is controlled. Exercise the failover path and capacity assumptions rather than relying on architecture diagrams alone.

e2e: Map required and optional dependencies for a user transaction.
Identify shared failure domains and quantify assumptions explicitly.
Design detection, spare capacity, and safe fallback or failover.
Validate degraded behavior and recovery through bounded tests and measured outcomes.

tasks.name: Calculate serial availability
steps: Two required independent services each have 99.9 percent availability over the same definition and window. Product availability is 0.999*0.999=0.998001, or 99.8001 percent. State independence explicitly; correlated outages and different measurement definitions invalidate treating this as an observed guarantee.

tasks.name: Calculate redundant capacity
steps: Three replicas each sustain forty requests per second. Normal peak is ninety. Losing one leaves eighty capacity, below demand by ten. The design has replica redundancy but insufficient failure headroom, so plan spare capacity, demand control, or a lower supported peak.

tasks.name: Identify common causes
steps: Two application zones share one regional database writer, one identity endpoint, and one deployment pipeline. Mark each shared failure path. Explain which risks a second zone mitigates and which require separate data, identity, or change-safety controls rather than more application Pods.

tasks.name: Design a safe fallback
steps: A product page depends on catalog, recommendations, and authorization. Allow missing recommendations with an explicit fallback, keep authorization enforced, and define catalog cache freshness. Explain how serving stale prices could violate business correctness even while HTTP availability appears improved.

key_terms: Required dependency: component necessary for the outcome.
Failure domain: scope sharing a common failure.
Headroom: capacity remaining after expected loss.
Common cause: event affecting supposedly redundant components.
lesson.safety: Use hypothetical dependencies; do not interrupt services or test failover on real writers.
cleanup: Discard the dependency graph and arithmetic; no infrastructure changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a three-replica multi-zone service still fails whenever identity is unavailable. What does that reveal about its availability model?
interview_points: Identity remains a required shared dependency.
Replica count does not remove common-cause paths.
Design bounded behavior without bypassing authorization and verify recovery capacity.

storyboard.title: Replicas cannot bypass a required shared dependency
storyboard.objective: Distinguish redundancy from independent service paths.

scenes.title: Serve through two replicas
scenes.caption: Both still require identity.
scenes.narration: Application replicas provide compute redundancy while sharing one authorization dependency.

scenes.title: Shared dependency fails
scenes.caption: Both paths lose a required function.
scenes.narration: Identity unavailability affects both replicas despite their separate placement.

scenes.title: Recover without bypass
scenes.caption: Correctness remains mandatory.
scenes.narration: A resilient authorized identity path or validated bounded policy restores service without skipping access checks.

sre/availability-design-and-dependency-f.core: Model complete required paths and common causes. Independence assumptions matter; replicas need failure headroom and safe detection. Optional fallback must never bypass essential correctness or authorization.
objectives: Find shared failure and capacity gaps
